title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6897 – Reuters estimate
body: The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The gap between each day's fixing and consensus estimates remains one of the clearest guides to how far the PBOC is willing to let the yuan run.--- The daily fixing is Beijing's quietest but clearest tool for telling markets how fast it wants the yuan to move, and after months of saying slow down, it has lately been saying go, gradually.Summary: The PBOC sets the daily USD/CNY reference rate, or midpoint, at around 0115 GMT, one of the most closely watched signals in Asian FX markets.

Despite hotter-than-expected inflation data, Treasury yields fell and yet tech stocks suffered all through the week. Is it a case of investors waking up to the struggles in market breadth and momentum? body: The direct market fallout is contained: QUBIC is a small-cap token, the loss is modest in dollar terms, and the selling has so far stayed confined to the token itself rather than spreading to the wider crypto market. The bigger near-term pressure is liquidity, with the network halted and exchanges suspending deposits and withdrawals, leaving holders unable to move tokens until the chain restarts. How the Computor vote handles restitution is likely to matter more for the token's recovery than the theft itself, since a clean, transparent outcome could steady confidence while a drawn-out freeze would add to doubts. title: USDCAD bounces after softer CPI data but they have work to do.
body: Canada's September CPI report gave traders a little something on both sides of the inflation debate. Headline inflation rose to 3.1% year over year from 3.0% in August, but came in below expectations of 3.2%. Meanwhile, inflation excluding gasoline slowed to 2.2% from 2.4%. Energy remains the problem area. Gasoline prices increased 27.8% from a year earlier, while fuel oil and other fuels surged 57.8%, with a greater impact on households in Atlantic Canada. Shelter inflation also accelerated, although rent growth held steady and mortgage interest costs continued to decline. The better news came from groceries. Annual inflation slowed to 1.7%, the lowest since May 2024, with fresh vegetables and sugar and confectionery prices declining from a year earlier. That is welcome relief, but slower inflation does not undo the earlier increases. Grocery prices remain 33.0% above September 2020 levels. What does it mean for the Bank of Canada? The headline moved higher, but energy drove the acceleration. The question for the Bank of Canada is whether those higher costs spread into other prices. Slower inflation excluding gasoline offers some reassurance. However, the 0.4% seasonally adjusted monthly increase warrants attention. For currency traders, higher inflation would normally support Canadian yields and the Canadian dollar, putting downward pressure on USDCAD. The softer-than-expected headline and slower non-gasoline inflation temper that argument.

At the same time, that's a negative for the Canadian dollar and we quickly saw USD/CAD rose to 1.4106 from 1.4075. USDCAD 10 mins: For background, Statistics Canada publishes the Consumer Price Index monthly, usually in the third week of the following month at 8:30 am ET. It measures price changes for a fixed basket of goods and services bought by Canadian households, covering shelter, food, transportation, household operations, clothing, health, recreation and alcohol and tobacco. Unlike in the US, the market's focus is the year-over-year change in the unadjusted index rather than the seasonally adjusted monthly change, though both are published. The Bank of Canada targets 2% total CPI inflation, the midpoint of a 1% to 3% control range, and its mandate is framed around that headline measure. Because headline inflation can be distorted by volatile items like gasoline and food, the Bank also watches its preferred core measures, CPI-trim and CPI-median. CPI-trim excludes the components with the most extreme price moves each month. CPI-median takes the price change at the 50th percentile of the basket. Markets often look at the average of the two.

title: Why do central banks target 2% inflation instead of 0%?
body: Most major central banks have a clearly defined inflation target around 2% per year over the medium term. But why they don't aim for 0%, so that prices remain unchanged over time? The answer lies in how inflation expectations influence economic decisions, the risks associated with deflation and the limitations of monetary policy. An inflation target provides a clear reference point for households, businesses and financial markets. This matters because expectations influence behaviour. Businesses consider expected inflation when setting prices and negotiating wages. Workers take expected changes in the cost of living into account when negotiating salaries. Households factor expected inflation into decisions about consumption, saving and borrowing, while investors incorporate it into bond yields and other asset prices. When the public trusts that a central bank will keep inflation close to its target, expectations are more likely to remain anchored around that level. This helps prevent temporary price shocks from turning into persistent inflation. Take the increase in oil prices as an example. Higher energy costs can push headline inflation up temporarily. If households and businesses believe the central bank will bring inflation back towards 2%, they may be less inclined to demand permanently higher wages or raise prices aggressively in anticipation of further inflation. This makes the initial shock less likely to spread throughout the economy.

title: Connecting the dots: What falling luxury sales could be telling us about the US economy
body: When most people look at designer bags, what do you think is the first thought that comes to mind? I'd wager it would be along the lines of "nice, but absolutely not at that price". And that very moment of hesitation could actually tell us more about the economy than you might think. Now, a luxury bag isn't like groceries or petrol. It is a want, not a need. But when people start thinking twice about those purchases, it is worth thinking about the bigger picture and whether consumer confidence is taking a hit. According to Citi's credit card data released earlier this month, luxury spending fell 6% year-on-year in September. And that follows from the declines of 4% in both July and August before that. The data shows three consecutive months of weakness. So, that is not exactly encouraging especially when wealthy US consumers have been one of the more resilient groups in this economy. Having said that, let's take a look at this. US retail sales actually rose by 0.8% in September, albeit largely bolstered by higher gasoline prices. But in excluding gasoline stations, retail sales still grew by 0.2%. It's not extravagant but it still suggests that US consumers are still spending. However, that doesn't necessarily mean they are buying more stuff. It just means that their spending habits have perhaps changed. So, how does this tie back to Wall Street? Just imagine that you are running a luxury retailer. You've got expensive stores, employees and marketing bills to pay.

title: Economic data spotlight: UK inflation set to climb as BOE rate hike and autumn budget collide
body: There's going to be plenty of watchful eyes on the UK CPI report this Wednesday, not least with the autumn budget just around the corner. Another hot set of inflation numbers could very well make life rather uncomfortable for both the government and the BOE. The headline annual inflation estimate is expected to rise to 3.4% in September, up from 3.1% in August. Meanwhile, core annual inflation is expected to also climb to 2.8% in September - up from 2.6% in the month before. All in all, that would take inflation further away from the BOE's 2% target, with higher energy costs continuing to put pressure on household budgets. At the same time, services inflation continues to be sticky and remains a problem for policymakers in trying to bring down broader price pressures in the UK economy. And while the UK economy isn't exactly falling apart, consumer demand remains fragile and the labour market has been showing signs of strain. The August GDP estimate may have surprised with 0.1% growth, but that was largely driven by the production side as services output was flat on the month. Meanwhile, the latest labour market snapshot showed that payrolls continued to fall in August - marking a 0.5% drop in the past year alone. The unemployment rate for July was seen at 4.9%, also up by 0.2% from the past year. So, that's making for a bit of an awkward combination for the BOE. It isn't all too worrying now but it could grow to be even more so if the diverging trends keep up.

title: Brokers must look beyond the crypto hype to where trading demand lies, says IC
body: The growing attention surrounding cryptocurrencies should not distract brokers from the markets their clients continue to trade, according to Jason Hughes, General Manager at IC. Speaking at iFX EXPO Asia 2026 in Hong Kong, Hughes joined industry executives to debate whether digital assets are delivering on their commercial promise, or whether established markets such as gold, precious metals and major FX pairs remain the backbone of the brokerage business. The discussion, "From Bitcoin to Bullion: Where Is the Real Revenue?", examined a question facing brokers across Asia and beyond: where should firms direct their next round of investment as client demand, trading technology and market conditions change? "For brokers, the priority is not choosing between traditional and digital assets. It is ensuring clients can access the markets they want to trade, supported by reliable infrastructure and consistent execution standards," Hughes said. While digital assets have opened new opportunities for brokers, the discussion also raised questions about the commercial case for investing in new products and technologies, particularly when established instruments continue to attract trading activity. The panel examined the challenges of 24/7 trading, from liquidity provision to execution quality, and the implications for brokers expanding their product offerings. For Hughes, the wider issue is how firms balance innovation with the fundamentals of their business.

title: Trump approval falls to record low. Poll shows Republicans losing badly in midterms
body: Republicans are running out of time to turn it around ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Trump is increasingly a liability of the party as his approval hits a record low of just 31%. It's an ugly chart as it continues to deteriorate with an inflection following the March war in Iran. Worse yet is the broader polling trend: Democrats lead Republicans 47% to 35% on the generic congressional ballot. That 12-point advantage is the largest of the current election cycle, according to Reuters/Ipsos. The generic ballot doesn't translate directly into seats but that is an uncomfortable gap for Republicans. If it carries through to election day, it points to an acrimonious final two years for Trump in the White House, including investigations on Epstein, the Iran war and corruption. For markets, it's likely that Democrat control of the House has been priced in for some time but a complete rout could kick off a broader repudation of Trump, even by his own party. That could strengthen the agenda for peace in the Middle East and an end to the trade war. At the same time, Trump under constant investigations could make him more impulsive and combative. There is also the question of how Trump responds to deteriorating polling and how he wants to manage his legacy. Does it encourage a more conciliatory approach aimed at delivering economic wins, or a harder push on his least-popular policies? Will he want to be remembered as the President that started an endless war with Iran?

title: USDJPY buyers land the punches, but sellers are still standing
body: Sellers have repeatedly defended the ceiling The USDJPY technical story since September 23 has centered on two key levels: the 50% midpoint of the decline from the July 2026 high to the September low at 158.419, and the 200-day moving average, currently at 158.565. The midpoint has remained fixed, while the 200-day moving average (higher green line) has edged higher from around 158.42. Together, they have created a resistance area where sellers have repeatedly leaned against the market and pushed the price lower. There have been at least 10 tests of that area, with three separate breaks above both technical levels. The highest reached 159.019 during the move that began on September 24. Another reached 158.72 on October 12. On each break, the buyers had their shot. Each time, they failed to sustain the momentum. The downside rotations have varied, with swing lows near 157.524 and 157.425 helping to define the lower portion of the battle. Most of the price action has stayed inside the red box on the chart. What the range teaches us An important lesson in my book Attacking Currency Trends is to use technical tools to define risk and judge who has control. When a recognizable midpoint and a longer-term moving average sit close together, they create a useful decision area. Sellers can lean against that area because it gives them a reference for where their trade starts to look wrong. Buyers know that getting above—and staying above—would strengthen their case.

title: CIBC cuts gold forecasts but still sees $5,500 in 2028
body: Gold bulls are getting a reminder that geopolitical turmoil doesn't always send bullion higher. Sometimes the inflation and interest-rate consequences overwhelm the safe-haven bid and sometimes the point of accumulating gold reserves is to use them when a shock -- like a war -- hits. That's the challenge running through CIBC's latest precious metals outlook. The bank has sharply lowered its forecasts as higher energy prices, a stronger US dollar and a more hawkish Federal Reserve complicate the trade. But it still sees a substantial recovery over the next two years. In its October report, CIBC cuts its 2027 average gold forecast to US$5,200 an ounce from $6,500. Its 2028 estimate falls to $5,500 from $6,000, while the fourth-quarter 2026 forecast drops to $4,500 from $6,500. Those are sizeable revisions but still leave CIBC comfortably above the consensus estimates included in the report: $4,620 for 2027 and $4,451 for 2028. "Despite this monetary policy headwind, we believe elevated geopolitical risk, fiscal concerns and continued diversification away from US Treasuries will underpin gold demand and support a recovery through 2027 and 2028," CIBC writes. Gold is at $4147 more than 25% below its early-year peak near $5,600. Against that reference point, its 2028 average forecast implies a recovery of roughly 29%. The problem is getting there.

title: Stock market shows an interesting hidden hint about investor confidence coming into earnings
body: Earnings season heats up: Are investors beginning to reward good results again? But fresh trading activity on October 19 suggests that sentiment may be stabilizing. With Netflix, Tesla and Meta preparing to report, the next question is whether investors are becoming more willing to reward strong corporate results, or whether this improvement is only temporary. Early earnings reactions were more negative than positive The third-quarter earnings reporting season, taking place during the fourth quarter of 2026, began with some uncomfortable signals for stock market bulls. Downside moves exceeding options-implied expectations outnumbered upside surprises by 11 to 6. Investors were not consistently rewarding corporate earnings announcements, even as individual companies continued reporting solid business performance. These observations matter because good earnings are not necessarily enough to make a stock rise. title: US NAHB housing market index 29 vs 31 prior
body: Priorw as 32 Current sales 33 vs 35 prior Sales over the next six months 32 vs 37 prior Prospective buyers 18 vs 23 prior The latest survey found that 43% of builders cut prices in October, the highest share during the 2020-2026 period. The average price cut remained at 6% for the seventh consecutive month. Meanwhile, 65% of builders reported using sales incentives in October, the 19th straight month at least 60% of builders have done so. This is a response to yet-another rise in borrowing costs, with US mortages nearing 7.5% on a 30-year fixed in the period. For background, The NAHB Housing Market Index is a monthly survey of homebuilder sentiment published by the National Association of Home Builders. It's released around mid-month at 10 am ET, usually the day before the government's housing starts report, which makes it the earliest read on the US housing market each month. The index is built from a survey of NAHB members, focused on builders of single-family homes. They rate three conditions: current sales of new homes, expected sales over the next six months and traffic of prospective buyers. The responses are combined into a headline index running from 0 to 100. A reading of 50 is the dividing line, with anything above it meaning more builders view conditions as good than poor. The traffic component historically runs well below the other two and rarely tops 50 even in strong markets.

title: Goldman Sachs estimates central banks bought 79 tonnes of gold in August, led by China
body: Steady central bank buying gives gold a source of demand that tends to be less sensitive to price than investment flows, which can help cushion pullbacks driven by speculative or ETF selling. That matters more now that bond yields are high across developed markets, a backdrop that would normally weigh on a non-yielding asset like gold. The pick-up in August suggests official buyers have not been deterred by elevated prices. For China, buying well above its reported additions would point to a continued push to diversify reserves away from the dollar. Geopolitical risk, including the Iran war, remains a parallel driver of safe-haven demand and could reinforce the official-sector bid. --- Earlier from GS: Goldman Sachs says rising global bond yields reflect a growing competition for capital --- Central banks are still buying gold at several times their old pace, and Goldman Sachs sees that steady official demand as a floor under the market rather than a passing phase. Summary: Goldman Sachs estimates central banks bought 79 tonnes of gold in August, Reuters reported. That is well above the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes a month. China was the largest identifiable buyer, with an estimated 25 tonnes. Goldman says it continues to see central bank demand as a structural support for gold. The August estimate is a sharp step up from Goldman's estimate of 44 tonnes for July. Goldman's estimate for China exceeds the roughly 20 tonnes the PBOC officially reported for August.

Oil is central to the outlook: Scotiabank flags the risk of an escalation in the Iran war after the US midterms, which could push energy and commodity prices higher and add to Canadian inflation pressure. Higher crude would normally support the Canadian dollar, but it would also strengthen the case for further tightening. If the Bank of Canada holds instead, the loonie would likely weaken, and markets could read the pause as a signal that policymakers are prepared to tolerate inflation near the top of the target range. - September's inflation report gave the Bank of Canada a softer headline to point to, but Scotiabank argues that summer travel coming off is no reason to hold rates while the forward-looking risks keep building. title: Morgan Stanley IM says bond yields are rising for the right reasons, favours US and Japan
body: Morgan Stanley IM's view offers a more benign reading of the yield rise than fears of fiscal strain or a growth scare, and if markets adopt it, US equities could keep absorbing higher yields as long as earnings deliver. The house's underweight in duration and preference for credit suggest it expects long-dated Treasuries to stay under pressure rather than rally. Its tilt toward Japan aligns with strong nominal growth there, while the underweight on Europe points to relative weakness in European stocks. For oil, the inflation component of high nominal growth is worth watching, since energy costs tied to the Iran war feed directly into it. The main risk to the thesis is a disappointing Q3 earnings season, which would remove the cushion Caron says is supporting equity prices. --- Earlier: Goldman Sachs says rising global bond yields reflect a growing competition for capital --- Morgan Stanley's investment arm reads the rise in Treasury yields as a sign that the US economy is running hot, and it is betting US earnings can stay one step ahead of borrowing costs. Summary: Morgan Stanley Investment Management, which oversees around $2 trillion, favours US and Japanese equities and is underweight Europe. Jim Caron, CIO of its Portfolio Solutions Group, says higher yields reflect resilient nominal growth rather than economic stress, with US real growth plus inflation running at about 6.5%. The US 10-year yield peaked at around 5.3% on 5 October this year before easing to around 5.1%.

title: Goldman Sachs says rising global bond yields reflect a growing competition for capital
body: If Goldman is right that higher yields reflect structural demand for capital rather than a temporary inflation scare, the pressure on long-dated bonds may prove persistent, keeping term premiums elevated across developed markets. For equities, the read-through is that index-level strength is resting heavily on earnings, so any disappointment from AI-linked leaders could expose valuations that have already compressed. Rising Japanese yields matter beyond Japan, since higher returns at home can draw domestic investors back from overseas markets and support the yen. Australian and UK bonds, already above 5%, stand out as the high-yield end of the developed world, which may support the Australian dollar and sterling on carry grounds. Higher government borrowing tied to energy security also links the bond story to oil, as elevated energy costs feed both fiscal needs and inflation risk. --- Earlier: Nasdaq and S&P rebounds; Dow slips --- Governments and AI builders are both lining up for funding, and Goldman Sachs argues that higher yields are simply the price investors are now charging to stand in that queue. Summary: Goldman Sachs says higher government bond yields have become the global norm, with 10-year yields up in every major developed market this year. Since January, 10-year yields have risen by around 100 bps in Japan, about 85 bps in the US and close to 80 bps in both the euro area and the UK.

Thursday's moving average break provided the catalyst The first step came on Thursday when the price moved away from the 100- and 200-hour moving averages (blue and green lines on the chart above). Those moving averages help define the shorter-term bias and give traders a reference for risk. When the price can move above both and build distance from them, it suggests sellers are losing some control and buyers are becoming more willing to step in. That move provided the catalyst. Friday's break above the swing area between 0.56225 and 0.5633 provided the next piece of technical evidence (see lower yellow area on the chart above). Friday's breakout gave buyers more confidence Why does that matter? Swing areas identify levels where buyers and sellers have previously made decisions. When the price moves above a former ceiling, it forces traders to reassess. Sellers leaning against that resistance lose some of their technical protection, while buyers gain a level they can use to define risk on a pullback.

title: China LPR preview: rates seen on hold for a 17th month after Q3 GDP beat
body: A hold is widely expected and should be largely priced, so any reaction is likely to come only from a surprise. An unexpected cut (not gonna happen... thats how unespected it'd be!) would probably weigh on the yuan, given the already wide gap between US and Chinese yields, while giving Chinese equities and property names a lift. The Australian and New Zealand dollars, often traded as proxies for Chinese growth, could firm on a cut as a sign of extra support for demand. For oil, any easing from the world's largest crude importer would be a modest positive for demand, at a time when Iran war disruptions are already keeping supply risk elevated. A hold keeps the focus on liquidity tools such as a reserve requirement ratio cut as the more likely form of any future easing. --- With growth back inside Beijing's target range and the Fed tightening, the PBOC has little reason to move its lending benchmarks and good reason to keep its powder dry. Summary: China's monthly loan prime rate fixing is due on Tuesday, with the one-year LPR expected to stay at 3.0% and the five-year at 3.5%. A hold would make it the 17th straight month without a change; both tenors were last cut in May 2025. The LPR is compiled from submissions by 20 designated banks; the one-year rate underpins most loans and the five-year rate guides mortgage pricing. The LPRs take their cue from the PBOC's seven-day reverse repo rate, its main policy rate since a mid-2024 framework change.
